an enthusiasm for following the Serchio towards its source, in accordance with earlier jour-
neys to the sources of rivers such as the Thames in 1815, since a stream flowing from near
the peak joins the Serchio in the valley below. But after his stay at Este, near Petrarch’s house
at Arquà (L ii 43), in September–October 1818, S. may have modelled his walk on that poet’s
solitary expedition to the summit of Mont Ventoux ‘to divert his thoughts’, as Mary later put it
(MSLL i 21). In addition, the resumption of work on her novel after the move to Bagni di San
Giuliano on 5 August 1820 raises the question of whether a new pretext for S.’s excursion was
to undertake a research visit on Mary’s behalf. According to a medieval tradition recorded
